name: Compounded GLP-1 route

card.summary: Obtaining semaglutide- or tirzepatide-type weight-loss drugs through compounding pharmacies, typically via online providers, to reach a leaner body.
card.note: Compounded drugs are not FDA-approved or reviewed for safety, effectiveness or quality; dosing errors are documented.

quick.overview:
The compounded GLP-1 route means getting GLP-1 receptor agonist drugs, such as semaglutide or tirzepatide, from compounding pharmacies rather than as approved branded products. The appeal is weight loss and a leaner look, often at a lower price or when branded supply was short.

The American Diabetes Association and the FDA have both published cautions about these products, and pharmacovigilance and market studies document adverse events and marketing practices.
quick.how: Typically a telehealth or online provider prescribes, and a state-licensed or outsourcing pharmacy prepares a formulation, sometimes with additives such as vitamin B12. This article does not cover doses or sourcing.
quick.risks: The FDA reports hundreds of adverse event reports for compounded semaglutide and tirzepatide, including dosing errors that led to hospitalization. Compounded products are not FDA-reviewed, and the agency warns about unapproved salt forms and fraudulent labelling.

lead: The compounded GLP-1 route is the practice of obtaining GLP-1 receptor agonist weight-loss drugs, chiefly semaglutide and tirzepatide, from compounding pharmacies instead of as branded, FDA-approved products. People use it to lose body fat and reach a leaner, more defined look, often because the branded drugs were scarce or expensive. It runs mostly through telehealth companies that prescribe online and route the order to a pharmacy that prepares its own version of the drug.[1][7][11]

The route grew out of the shortages of Ozempic, Wegovy, Mounjaro and Zepbound that began in 2022. While a drug is on the FDA shortage list, pharmacies may prepare close copies of it under federal conditions, and a large direct-to-consumer market formed around that window.[11][12][14] The American Diabetes Association says compounded versions bypass regulatory measures and continue to be heavily marketed even as shortages resolve.[1] In January 2026 Novo Nordisk's chief executive said up to 1.5 million people in the United States were using compounded GLP-1 drugs.[11]

The route is discussed in physique and fat-loss communities because GLP-1 drugs lower appetite, and published trials of the approved products report large average weight loss: about 15 percent of body weight over 68 weeks for semaglutide and roughly 15 to 21 percent over 72 weeks for tirzepatide, depending on dose.[11][12] The FDA states that compounded drugs are not FDA-approved and are not reviewed for safety, effectiveness or quality, and a body of pharmacovigilance and market research documents adverse events, labelling problems and marketing practices.[3][10]

chain: Prescription via telehealth and compounding pharmacy
Weight and body-fat loss, leaner appearance
angle.text: People use the route to reach GLP-1 weight loss when branded products are costly or short. The documented trade-off involves quality, dosing and reporting concerns.

paras: Compounded GLP-1 products are made by pharmacies that prepare a drug to a prescription instead of purchasing a finished product from the original manufacturer. Wikipedia describes compounding as the preparation of customised medications for needs that mass-produced versions cannot meet, such as removing an ingredient a patient cannot take or supplying a drug in short supply.[13]

Two kinds of facility are involved under the 2013 Drug Quality and Security Act. Section 503A pharmacies prepare patient-specific preparations under state pharmacy regulation, while section 503B outsourcing facilities do bulk compounding and are regulated directly by the FDA.[13] The law was passed after the 2012 fungal meningitis outbreak traced to the New England Compounding Center, which reportedly sickened about 750 people.[13]

In the GLP-1 market, a typical customer fills in an online questionnaire for a telehealth company, a clinician issues a prescription, and a partner pharmacy prepares and ships the product. A JAMA analysis of prescription monitoring data described compounded weight-loss prescriptions, self-payment, out-of-state dispensing and the ingredients in the products, including vitamin B12 added to some formulations.[4] A Colorado survey of direct-to-consumer provider websites examined how common the providers were and what their advertising said.[7]

The FDA declared a shortage of Ozempic and Wegovy (semaglutide) in August 2022 and a tirzepatide shortage in December 2022.[11][12] Federal law lets compounders prepare essentially a copy of a branded drug while it appears on the shortage list, which allowed telehealth firms and aesthetic-medicine clinics to offer compounded semaglutide and tirzepatide at prices below the branded products.[3][14][15] High prices and limited insurance coverage are the factors researchers most often name behind the market.[7][16]

Tirzepatide was declared out of shortage in October 2024, though enforcement was delayed to the end of that year after a lawsuit by compounding pharmacies. The semaglutide shortage ended in spring 2025, after which compounding was again limited to a narrow individual-patient exception.[12][14] An Expert Opinion on Drug Safety paper, an American Journal of Health-System Pharmacists article and a JAMA Health Forum study address the market after the shortages ended.[3][16][17]

Large telehealth firms, with Hims & Hers the most publicised, sold compounded semaglutide injections. According to a law-firm summary, the FDA sent Hims a warning letter in September 2025 over claims it considered false or misleading, and Hims was on pace for about $725 million in 2025 revenue from its weight-loss category, including branded and compounded products.[14] A second law-firm summary reports that the FDA sent about 100 cease-and-desist letters in September 2025 over deceptive advertising for compounded drugs.[18]

On February 5, 2026, Hims announced a compounded semaglutide pill. Novo Nordisk accused the company of illegal mass compounding, the FDA commissioner said the agency would take swift action against mass-marketed copycat drugs, and the Department of Health and Human Services said it had referred Hims to the Department of Justice. Hims announced on February 7 that it would stop offering the pill.[14] On February 20, 2026 the FDA sent thirty warning letters to telehealth companies and online clinics alleging false or misleading labeling and advertising, and on March 9 Novo Nordisk and Hims & Hers announced a partnership under which Hims would offer branded Ozempic and Wegovy and stop most advertising of compounded GLP-1 products, with Novo dismissing its patent suit while reserving the right to refile.[18]

Hacker News discussions of the period carried headlines such as 'The end of compounded GLP-1 drugs leaves many patients in a lose-lose position' and 'Hims cancels plans to sell compounded GLP-1 pill after FDA backlash,' reflecting how the rule changes were followed outside medical journals.[19][20]

The FDA says compounding is appropriate only when an approved drug cannot meet a patient's medical need, and that patients should use a prescription filled at a state-licensed pharmacy.[10] Its page lists telehealth red flags, including deep discounts, no clinician screening, and misspelled labels or wrong pharmacy addresses.[10]

The FDA states that retatrutide and cagrilintide cannot be used in compounding under federal law because they are not components of an approved drug, and that it has sent warning letters to telehealth companies, ingredient distributors and outsourcing facilities.[10] It says semaglutide sodium and semaglutide acetate are different active ingredients from the one in approved products and that it knows of no lawful basis for using them in compounding.[10] A green-list import alert, 66-80, targets GLP-1 ingredients with potential quality concerns without limiting lawful compounding.[10]

Under federal law, as summarised by a law firm, compounding essentially a copy of a branded drug is allowed if the drug is on the shortage list, or through an exception for a change made for an identified patient that the prescriber judges significant. Hims argued its liposomal formulation fell under that exception, while Novo disputed it.[14] Wikipedia notes that FDA guidance in 2026 allowed a broader definition of copy for custom-compounded agents.[13]

Semaglutide mimics the gut hormone GLP-1 and reduces appetite; tirzepatide additionally acts on the GIP receptor, which makes it a dual agonist.[12] In a phase III trial of 1,961 adults with obesity, semaglutide produced a 14.9 percent weight change over 68 weeks against 2.4 percent with placebo, alongside lifestyle intervention.[11] In a phase III trial of adults without diabetes, tirzepatide produced mean changes of about 15.0, 19.5 and 20.9 percent at 72 weeks across its three tested doses, against 3.1 percent for placebo.[12]

These figures describe the approved, manufactured products. Wikipedia reports that people regained about 67 percent of lost weight within a year of stopping semaglutide in a 2025 systematic review, and that lean body mass fell by 0 to 40 percent of the total loss in some studies, though lean-to-total ratio rose in all of them.[11] Physique-minded users therefore tend to pair the drugs with resistance training and protein.

A pharmacovigilance study of the FDA Adverse Event Reporting System from 2018 to 2024 found that 707 of 81,078 reports for liraglutide, semaglutide and tirzepatide involved compounded products. Compounded products had higher reporting odds for abdominal pain, diarrhea, nausea, cholecystitis, preparation errors, contamination and hospitalization, and lower odds for administration and dosing errors.[3] The paper also reported higher reporting odds for suicidality; Wikipedia notes that in January 2026 the FDA asked for removal of the suicidal behavior and ideation warning from GLP-1 medications, reflecting an ongoing debate about that signal.[3][12]

The FDA reports multiple adverse events, some requiring hospitalization, tied to dosing errors with compounded injectable semaglutide, caused by patients measuring doses wrongly or clinicians miscalculating. It reports symptoms such as nausea, vomiting, diarrhea, abdominal pain and constipation after use above the labelled amount.[10] As of May 31, 2026 the agency had received 990 reports for compounded semaglutide and more than 730 for compounded tirzepatide, and notes that under-reporting is likely because most state-licensed pharmacies are not required to report.[10] Other work has looked at accidental overdoses, poison-control exposure trends and primary care documentation of compounded use.[5][21][22]

The FDA says some fraudulent products carry false labels, naming pharmacies that do not exist or licensed pharmacies that did not make the product, and it reports an adverse event tied to a product labelled as compounded tirzepatide from a pharmacy that had not compounded it.[10] It has warned about counterfeit Ozempic and about products sold 'for research purposes' or 'not for human consumption,' including semaglutide, tirzepatide, retatrutide, survodutide and mazdutide.[10] Counterfeit Ozempic pens in Europe in October 2023 were reported to have caused hospitalisations for low blood sugar and seizures.[11]

The FDA advises discarding a multi-dose vial within 28 days of first use and keeping injectable products refrigerated.[10] Side effects of the approved drugs include gastrointestinal symptoms, gallstones, and, for semaglutide, a boxed US warning for thyroid C-cell tumors based on rodent studies.[11]

On T Nation, users in cutting threads discuss GLP-1 drugs alongside training and other compounds. One poster described using telehealth clinics that mostly work with compounding pharmacies, and also buying from peptide sites, saying they saw little difference beyond lower prices and filler content.[23] Another thread, titled around a drug called retatrutide, features replies arguing that these compounds act directly on hunger signalling rather than on willpower.[24] A cutting-log thread asks about balancing a GLP-1 with testosterone to keep muscle while losing fat.[25]

Forum users commonly cite price and availability as reasons to choose the compounded route. Commenters in the same spaces also raise purity and labelling, which mirrors the FDA's concerns about unapproved and research-labelled versions.[10][23]

Journal commentary has taken several angles. JAMA Health Forum viewpoints discuss marketing and consumer protection, and the Journal of General Internal Medicine published an editorial on how clinicians can talk to patients about compounded products.[6][8][26] Pharmacy-practice authors discuss balancing access and safety after the shortages, and a Missouri Medicine article reviews the future of the route.[16][27]

Supporters of compounding argue it widens access for people who cannot afford branded products. Regulators and medical societies respond that the products are not reviewed and that supply no longer qualifies for the shortage provision.[1][10]

Trials of compounded products themselves are limited. A registered early phase 1 study of microdosed GLP-1 for longevity and quality-of-life measures is enrolling by invitation (NCT07092605, planned n=150, started November 2024), and a prospective cohort of a GLP-1 medication plus behavioral health program is registered but not yet recruiting.[9][28] Published work on the compounded route is mostly pharmacovigilance and market surveys.[3][7]
The weight-loss figures above come from trials of the approved drugs, which are the evidence base for the active ingredients.[11][12]

timeline.event: Fungal meningitis outbreak linked to the New England Compounding Center prompts tighter compounding law.[13]
Drug Quality and Security Act creates the 503A and 503B framework.[13]
FDA declares shortages of Ozempic/Wegovy (August) and tirzepatide (December), opening the shortage-list compounding provision.[11][12]
Counterfeit Ozempic pens reported in Europe; FDA issues a warning in December.[11]
FDA declares the tirzepatide shortage over in October; enforcement delayed to year-end after a pharmacy lawsuit.[12]
Semaglutide shortage ends in spring; FDA sends warning letters over compounded GLP-1 marketing in September.[14]
Hims & Hers announces then withdraws a compounded semaglutide pill (February 5-7); HHS refers the company to the Justice Department.[14]
FDA sends thirty warning letters to telehealth firms (February 20); Novo Nordisk and Hims & Hers announce a partnership (March 9).[18]
FDA reports 990 adverse event reports for compounded semaglutide and over 730 for tirzepatide as of May 31.[10]

lore.intro: In physique forums the compounded route is discussed as a cheaper or more available way to get GLP-1 fat loss, with threads about telehealth clinics, peptide sites and pairing the drugs with training.[23][25]

claims.claim: Compounded GLP-1 is the same as the branded drug at a lower price
claims.believers: Users say clinic-prepared products have worked comparably for them and cost much less than branded versions.[23]
claims.experts: The FDA says compounded drugs are not reviewed for safety, effectiveness or quality, and that some forms use salts it knows of no lawful basis for.[10]

claims.claim: Telehealth compounding pharmacies are regulated, so the product is safe
claims.believers: A forum poster notes that clinics mostly use compounding pharmacies that have regulatory oversight.[23]
claims.experts: State boards oversee 503A pharmacies, and the FDA notes most are not required to report adverse events, so reports likely undercount problems.[10][13]

claims.claim: Peptide sites sell the same compounds more cheaply
claims.believers: One user reports little difference between clinic and peptide-site products beyond lower price and fewer fillers.[23]
claims.experts: The FDA warns about products sold as 'for research purposes' or 'not for human consumption,' and about fraudulent labels.[10]

claims.claim: GLP-1 drugs reduce appetite directly, so willpower is not the factor
claims.believers: Replies in a retatrutide thread say the compounds act on hunger signalling in the body and brain.[24]
claims.experts: Trials of approved semaglutide and tirzepatide report mean weight reductions of roughly 15 to 21 percent over 68 to 72 weeks.[11][12]

claims.claim: Combining a GLP-1 with training and other compounds preserves muscle
claims.believers: Cutting-thread posters discuss stacking the drugs with testosterone to maintain or add muscle.[25]
claims.experts: A 2024 review summarised on Wikipedia found lean mass loss of 0 to 40 percent of total loss in some studies, with lean-to-total ratio rising.[11] No trial of the stack was found.

claims.claim: Microdosed GLP-1 improves longevity and quality-of-life measures
claims.believers: Proponents of microdosing describe interest in mood, inflammation and longevity measures, the conditions listed in a registered trial.[9]
claims.experts: A registered early phase 1 trial is enrolling and has not reported results.[9]

claims.claim: Compounded versions carry added risk of dosing errors and contamination
claims.believers: Critics in the community raise purity and labelling concerns.[23]
claims.experts: FAERS analysis found higher odds of preparation errors, contamination and hospitalization for compounded reports, and the FDA describes dosing errors needing hospitalization.[3][10]
